opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's really at the heart of what we think about with inference. The traditional view, especially coming from the GPU world, is that you trade one for the other: you batch more requests together to keep the hardware busy and get good throughput, but every individual user waits longer. For a lot of modern AI workloads, especially agentic systems where one model call feeds the next, that tradeoff becomes really painful, because latency compounds across the chain.

So with the SN40L, the way we approached it was to ask: where does the latency actually come from? For large language model inference, particularly the decode phase, you're fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. Every token you generate requires streaming the model weights through the compute. If you're doing that kernel by kernel, the way a GPU typically does, you're constantly going back out to HBM, writing intermediate results, reading them back in, and paying kernel launch overheads. That's where a lot of the latency goes.

Our reconfigurable dataflow architecture lets us fuse an entire decoder layer, or even multiple layers, into a single dataflow pipeline on the chip. The intermediate data stays on-chip in our distributed SRAM and flows directly from one operation to the next. That gets us much closer to the theoretical peak memory bandwidth utilization, which means lower latency per token even at small batch sizes. You don't need huge batches just to amortize overheads.

The other piece is the memory hierarchy. The SN40L has three tiers: on-chip SRAM, HBM, and a large pool of DDR. That DDR capacity matters a lot for the tradeoff, because it lets us hold many models, or a composition of experts, on a single node and switch between them very quickly. So instead of getting throughput by batching many users onto one model, you can serve many different models efficiently, with HBM acting as a fast cache for whatever's active.

So the way I'd summarize it is that we try not to accept the tradeoff as a given. By getting the dataflow right and getting the memory system right, you can push the whole Pareto frontier out, so you get high tokens per second for an individual user while still getting good aggregate throughput and efficiency for the system. Then, depending on the deployment, whether it's interactive agents or offline batch processing, you can choose where you want to operate on that frontier.

r001.rationale: The response attributes lower token latency to fused dataflow pipelines and on-chip SRAM, but does not identify low-latency matrix–vector computation as the reason for token-generation speed.

r002.rationale: It says SN40L can achieve lower latency at small batch sizes and does not need huge batches to amortize overhead, but does not state that increasing batch size raises latency less on SN40L than on GPUs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the central tension in inference, and I think it gets misunderstood a lot. Everybody wants to quote tokens per second per user, and everybody wants to quote total tokens per second for the system, and those are pulling in opposite directions on a conventional architecture.

The way to think about it is: what does a GPU have to do to get good throughput? It has to batch. It takes a bunch of users' requests, stacks them up, and runs them through the matrix multiplies together so that the weights it pulls out of memory get reused across many tokens. That's the only way to amortize the memory bandwidth cost of streaming the model weights. And the cost of that is latency. Each individual user is now waiting on the batch, and the time per token for any one of them goes up. So on a GPU, if you want low latency, you run small batches and your utilization collapses. If you want throughput, you batch and every user's experience gets worse. You're picking a point on that curve.

With SN40L, what we tried to do is change the shape of the curve rather than just pick a different point on it. A few things go into that.

The first is the dataflow architecture itself. Instead of the kernel-by-kernel execution model, where you run a matmul, write the result back to HBM, read it back in, run the next operation, we map the whole decoder layer, or multiple layers, spatially onto the chip. The intermediate activations flow from one unit to the next through on-chip memory. So you're not paying that round trip to external memory between every operator, and that removes a big chunk of the per-token latency that has nothing to do with the actual arithmetic.

The second is the memory hierarchy. SN40L has three tiers: a lot of on-chip SRAM, then HBM, and then a large DDR capacity, which is what lets us hold many models or very large models resident. The trick for decode is that when you're generating a token, the work is dominated by reading the weights, not by compute. So being able to keep the hot parts of the model in the fast tiers and stream through them efficiently means that even at batch size one, we're getting high effective bandwidth. That's where the high tokens-per-second-per-user numbers come from. We're not relying on batching to hide memory latency the way a GPU has to.

And the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that because the dataflow mapping is static and the compiler knows the whole graph, we can be much more deliberate about how we allocate resources. The compiler can decide that these units are dedicated to attention, these to the MLP, this is how activations move between them, and there's no runtime scheduling overhead fighting for the same hardware. That determinism matters a lot for tail latency, which is really what users feel.

Now, I don't want to pretend the tradeoff disappears. If you have many concurrent users, you still want to serve them efficiently, and we do batch. But the slope is different. Adding users degrades per-user latency much more gently, because the baseline per-token cost is already low and we're not depending on batching to be efficient in the first place. So in practice you can run at a batch size that gives you genuinely fast interactive responses and still have good system throughput, instead of having to choose.

The reason I think this matters more and more is that the workloads are shifting. With agentic systems, with reasoning models that generate thousands of tokens before they give you an answer, the latency of a single stream becomes the bottleneck for the whole application. If every step of an agent is waiting on a slow decode, batching across users doesn't help you at all. So I'd argue that over the next couple of years, per-stream latency is going to be the thing that actually determines whether these applications are usable, and that's really the design point we optimized for.

r001.rationale: The response attributes speed to dataflow execution, reduced external-memory round trips, and effective bandwidth at batch size one, but does not identify low-latency matrix–vector computation as the cause.

r002.rationale: It says adding users degrades per-user latency “much more gently” on SN40L, contrasting this with GPUs’ latency-throughput tradeoff.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that latency and throughput have to be considered together, in the context of the application. If you’re interacting with a model, you care about how quickly the first token comes back and how quickly subsequent tokens arrive. If you’re running a large offline workload, you may care much more about the total number of tokens you can process per second.

Batching is one way to increase throughput, because you can reuse model weights across multiple requests. But waiting to form a batch, or making that batch too large, can increase latency. So maximizing throughput by itself isn’t necessarily the right objective. You want to maximize throughput while meeting the response-time requirements of the application.

For a system like SN40L, that means thinking about computation, memory, and data movement together. Where are the weights? Where is the attention state? How do you keep the compute resources supplied with data? And you have to distinguish the initial processing of the prompt from generating tokens one at a time, because those put different demands on the system.

So there isn’t one operating point that’s optimal for everything. The goal is to use the hardware and software together to deliver as much useful throughput as possible within the latency budget the user actually cares about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prompt and token-generation demands but does not attribute SN40L’s token-generation speed to low-latency matrix–vector computation.

r002.rationale: It says batching can increase throughput and latency, but makes no claim that larger batches cause a smaller latency increase on SN40L systems than on GPUs.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that latency and throughput have to be considered together. You want to serve a lot of requests, but each user still expects a responsive experience. So the objective is really to maximize throughput within a latency requirement, rather than maximize throughput in isolation.

For inference, there are also two different phases. Processing the prompt gives you opportunities for parallel computation. Generating tokens is sequential, and moving the model’s weights and intermediate state becomes a major consideration. Batching can improve efficiency, but waiting to assemble a batch or making it too large can hurt responsiveness.

With SN40L, our approach is to use the dataflow architecture and memory hierarchy to keep computation supplied with data and reduce unnecessary movement. That gives us more room to deliver throughput while maintaining low latency. But the operating point depends on the workload: an interactive conversation has different requirements from an offline job. You have to measure the system against that actual experience—time to first token, time between tokens, and how those behave as you add concurrent users.

r001.rationale: It describes token generation as sequential and mentions SN40L’s dataflow architecture and memory hierarchy, but does not attribute its speed to low-latency matrix–vector computation.

r002.rationale: It says batching can improve efficiency while hurting responsiveness, but makes no comparison of how batch size affects latency on SN40L versus GPUs.
